The ~5x wage increase comes with an ~8x rise in output per worker and a gross savings rate going from ~20% to ~40% (?) of output if I have that right? The wage gain therefore then seems to be mostly produced by the productivity event.

One of the biggest killers of innovation is being blinded by hypothetical downsides. It’s easy to raise concerns about why something might be risky. It's much harder to consider the potential harm of putting too many restrictions in place.

Consider the de facto ban on nuclear with the establishment of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Today we'd have a modern, robust electric grid, and much higher economic growth, if we had kept building nuclear power plants.

All around us we see systems that were well-intentioned when they were introduced, but had unintended consequences.

How things fail:
- Asymmetric error costs - approve a bad reactor or drug and you’re famous. Yet if you block a good one, no one ever knows.

- Process as a veto - hourly fees, multi-step license applications, EPA reviews. Endless delays erode capital.

- Worst-case models treated as fact - LNT radiation, any sonic boom is unacceptable, etc.

- Rules written for the last accident, applied to the next design - we see this in everything from nuclear to financial services.

Change is uncomfortable, but if we stop progress, we do a disservice to our ancestors who tolerated discomfort to bring us the modern age. We owe it to them to continue making progress.

Keep building.

September 30, 2026

I bought heavily into HydroGraph before today’s close. The selling looked to me like short pressure triggering stop losses—and I used the weakness to increase my position.

Why such strong conviction? Look at the commercial setup entering Q4.

🔹 Larger orders on the horizon. HydroGraph’s latest MD&A says customer discussions are expected to generate larger purchase orders AND a long-term supply agreement within calendar 2026. Management still has to deliver, but that makes the coming quarter particularly interesting.

🔹 Plastics alone offer enormous potential. Automotive components, packaging, electronics and consumer goods all need lighter, stronger, more durable materials. HydroGraph reports thermoplastic test examples showing 30% higher strength at break and 60% greater toughness. These are benefits manufacturers have a reason to evaluate.

🔹 The commercial infrastructure is taking shape. Hubron, Broadway, Modern Dispersions and Midland are qualified compounding partners—helping integrate graphene into usable polymer formulations and providing routes into established industrial supply chains.

🔹 Fresh evidence from coatings. Sparc’s September 15 announcement reported a 25% improvement in corrosion resistance in 16-week solvent-based coating tests using HydroGraph graphene. Longer testing is due in November; positive results would lead to commercial supply negotiations.

🔹 Defense adds another major opportunity. HydroGraph is pursuing applications across government, aerospace and defense, with former Hexcel executive Dr. Robert Yancey developing those relationships. Qualification takes time, but the potential extends across advanced composites, coatings and other demanding applications.

What excites me is the breadth: automotive, plastics, coatings, concrete, thermal management, etc. There is so much, just take a look at the graphics below to get an idea. The paste and compounding strategy help customers overcome the practical barriers to adoption.

My conviction is that successful adoption in even a few of these markets could create a substantial recurring business. Meaningful orders still need to land, but the groundwork is increasingly tangible.

What happens when one major manufacturer qualifies an additive that improves its products—and competitors need to catch up?

That’s the possibility I’m buying into.

It might seem like people in tech and investing have lost their minds. And in some sense that is true. But a lot of the behavior is rational in some sense, even if it’s not “honorable” 

Why is it happening now? Yes, some people have AI psychosis. But something deeper is happening 

In life, there are two types of games. Single turn and multi turn games. Single turn, or one-shot, games are just what they sound like. One turn and the game is over. No more turns. 

Multi turn, or sequential, games have multiple turns. Which means history, reputation, and consequences for your actions have a large impact. You expect to see the players on the board multiple times in the future 

Most things in the game of life are multi turn. Careers are long. Investments take time to come to fruition, and you will want to redeploy the capital 

But when the stakes get high enough, people start to squint at the board and see that they can end the game in one turn. Or at least they think they can. 

I’ve talked a lot about how AI is the big one. So it’s not crazy to me that some people are looking at the board and thinking there might be only one turn left, and they are just going for it.

Micron Q4: five takeaways

1) Korea called it, again. Three weeks ago the first-ten-day export data set a record while everyone was busy calling the peak in AI. Micron just printed $54.2bn of revenue, +379% year-on-year, beat consensus by $3bn, and guided the next quarter to $61.5bn against a street at $57bn. And note that Q4 was a 14-week quarter, so the Q1 guide on a normal 13-week quarter is an even bigger sequential step than the headline suggests. The earnings cycle is not slowing. It is accelerating into a market that has spent the summer compressing multiples.

2) The cyclicality debate is over, for now. This is the argument we have had for many months: is memory still a boom-bust commodity? Gross margin at 87% and roughly $100bn of remaining performance obligations across the strategic customer agreements say the business has changed. Contracts do not remove the cycle, they stretch it. And $33bn of free cash flow in the quarter, $73bn of cash on the balance sheet: they fund the Idaho buildout and return the excess without touching the debt markets. That is the one thing the neoclouds cannot say.

3) Valuation is still absurd. On the new Q1 guide, run-rate EPS is about $153. At $1,070 that is roughly 7x. The S&P is on 22x. CrowdStrike is near 200x. The market is still pricing memory profits as if they end next year; the guidance says they rise into 2027, when HBM4 volume lands. Way, way too cheap remains the verdict.

4) It confirms the book. Quality of earnings is the factor in a hiking cycle, and Micron is the definition of it. Memory is the all-weather asset in the frontier-slows debate: training wants bandwidth, inference wants capacity, and both showed up in this print. US memory over Korea into the licence decision. We hold. We do not add after a 290% run.

5) The number to watch is capex. FY26 capex was $27bn against $62bn of free cash flow. If all three memory makers raise capex sharply at once, that is the first 2027-28 warning sign. Management already flagged that the rate of price increases is moderating, which means volume and contracts are now doing the work rather than price. That is exactly what you want if you own it for durability rather than for the spike. We do.

After 3 years building LLM agents, I think the model people actually choose to run says a lot, it’s a bit like voting with your credit card. That’s why the benchmark I pay the most attention to is usage on OpenRouter.

For smaller/cheaper models, DeepSeek Flash is doing ~22.7T tokens a week, GLM Flash ~10.6T and GPT-6 Luna ~5.1T, which gives you a pretty good idea of where people are finding value for money.

For larger, frontier models, Opus 5.5 is at ~1.9T and GPT-6 Sol ~1.2T, while Gemini Pro is at ~0.2T, roughly 10x less volume than Opus.

Obviously cheaper models will consume more tokens, so you have to compare within each category, but I find this much more useful than another benchmark showing a model winning by 2 points. You can game a benchmark but not where companies are spending their $$$.

And that still only gives you the global trend. For your product, the eval that matters is your own, on actual customer tasks, because a model can be amazing overall and still suck at the specific thing you need it to do.

That’s why I think you want a multi-model platform, with customer evals driving which model handles which task, so you can improve quality and optimize your token stack as the models change. You shouldn’t be married to one model.

When software becomes a commodity, the moat is how much value you deliver per unit of compute.

Anyone can build the same features. Few can serve as many users, across as many use cases, without restrictive limits.

Model quality compounds that advantage: better results with less compute mean higher gross margins and more compute to train the next, more efficient model.

That’s the winning flywheel for the next 24 months.
